title: Grade 5 Science — Wed, Jun 18
description: Respiratory System — Day 3 of 5: Mechanism of breathing — inhalation and exhalation
subject: science

questions.question: Inhalation (breathing in) occurs when:
options: The diaphragm relaxes and chest shrinks
The diaphragm contracts (flattens) and chest expands, creating low pressure
The diaphragm moves up and chest shrinks
questions.explanation: During inhalation: diaphragm contracts (flattens downward), intercostal muscles pull ribs up and out → chest volume increases → pressure inside drops → air rushes in.

questions.question: Exhalation (breathing out) occurs when:
options: The diaphragm contracts and chest expands
The diaphragm relaxes (domes up) and chest volume decreases, creating high pressure
questions.explanation: During exhalation: diaphragm relaxes (domes up), ribs move down and inward → chest volume decreases → pressure increases → air is pushed out.

questions.question: Air flows FROM high pressure to low pressure. During INHALATION, the pressure inside the chest is:
options: Lower than outside air — so air flows in
questions.explanation: Inhalation increases chest volume → decreases internal pressure → pressure inside < outside → air flows IN (from high to low pressure).

questions.question: During EXHALATION, the pressure inside the chest is:
options: Higher than outside air — so air flows out
questions.explanation: Exhalation decreases chest volume → increases internal pressure → pressure inside > outside → air flows OUT.

questions.question: The DIAPHRAGM's position during INHALATION:
questions.explanation: During inhalation: diaphragm CONTRACTS → moves DOWNWARD (flattens). This increases the chest cavity volume.

questions.question: The DIAPHRAGM's position during EXHALATION:
questions.explanation: During exhalation: diaphragm RELAXES → moves UPWARD (domes). This decreases chest volume and pushes air out.

questions.question: The ribcage movement during INHALATION is:
options: Ribs move outward and upward — increasing chest volume
questions.explanation: Intercostal muscles pull ribs outward and upward during inhalation → chest expands → more room for air.

questions.question: A balloon model of the lungs (jar, balloon, rubber membrane) demonstrates that pulling the rubber membrane DOWNWARD:
questions.explanation: Pulling the rubber membrane (diaphragm) down increases jar volume → pressure drops → balloon (lung) inflates. This models inhalation.

questions.question: Forced exhalation (like blowing out a candle) is helped by:
options: Abdominal muscles contracting, pushing diaphragm up further
questions.explanation: In forced exhalation, abdominal muscles contract → push contents upward → push diaphragm up further → greater pressure → more air expelled.

questions.question: A healthy adult inhales approximately ___ litres of air per breath at rest:
questions.explanation: Tidal volume ≈ 0.5 litres (500 mL) per breath at rest. During deep breathing it can reach 3–5 litres (vital capacity).

questions.question: Vital capacity is:
options: The air remaining after full exhalation
The maximum amount of air you can exhale after a maximum inhalation
questions.explanation: Vital capacity is the maximum air you can forcefully exhale after a maximum inhalation. It is about 4.5–5 litres in a healthy adult.

questions.question: Residual volume is:
options: The air that always remains in the lungs even after full exhalation
questions.explanation: Even after a maximum exhalation, about 1.2 litres of air remains in the lungs. This is residual volume — it keeps the alveoli from collapsing.

questions.question: Why can't we exhale ALL the air from our lungs?
options: Residual volume always stays to prevent alveoli from collapsing
questions.explanation: If alveoli collapsed completely, they would be very hard to re-inflate. Residual volume keeps them slightly inflated, ready for the next breath.

questions.question: A person drowning who inhales water struggles because:
options: Water is less dense than air
Water cannot participate in gas exchange at alveoli — the alveoli cannot extract O₂ from water
There is no oxygen in water
questions.explanation: Alveoli are designed for gas exchange with AIR. Water in alveoli blocks oxygen transfer to blood — the person gets no oxygen despite breathing.

questions.question: Hiccups are caused by:
options: Eating too fast causes stomach to expand, irritating the diaphragm and causing sudden contractions
questions.explanation: Eating quickly or carbonated drinks can irritate the diaphragm, causing sudden involuntary contractions. The closing of the vocal cords produces the 'hic' sound.
